newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia sees Fokker deal as dead.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia sees Fokker deal as dead.

text.p: Malaysia does not expect a proposed rescue of bankrupt Dutch planemaker Fokker to proceed, Deputy Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said on Wednesday.
"We entered into serious negotiations but I don't think we can proceed any longer," Anwar, who is also finance minister, told reporters.
Ministry of Finance Secretary-General Clifford Herbert further said that the problem was Stork NV's demand that Malaysia put up money first before allowing a due diligence study of Fokker.

Engineering and industrial services group Stork owns the profitable Fokker aircraft maintenance and components units. It announced on Monday that it was no longer bound by a memorandum of understanding, signed in March, as the blueprint for the possible resurrection of the planemaker.
"Without due diligence, we cannot make a financial commitment," Herbert told reporters. Due diligence refers to a thorough audit to assess the financial viability of a company.
The company's court-appointed receivers had said Stork blamed its pull-out on the failure of Malaysia's state investment arm Khazanah Nasional Bhd to guarantee sufficient financial support.
The memorandum of understanding was designed to provide a common position for negotiations with Malaysia, which emerged as a potential suitor last month.
All parties had planned to complete their talks by May 1.

Malaysia was just one in a string of possible suitors for Fokker, and was widely seen as the planemaker's final lifeline. Tentative rescue plans had assumed Malaysia would invest 450 million guilders in a new Fokker.
Fokker went bankrupt a year ago after majority shareholder Daimler Benz pulled the plug, saying it could no longer sustain the planemaker's huge financial losses.
Without the Malaysian deal, Fokker's plant is expected to be closed for good this summer and the assets liquidated.
